clinicalPearls: Steatorrhea (fecal fat excretion >7% of dietary fat) is a common manifestation of malabsorption, producing large, bulky, malodorous stools; malabsorptive diarrhea is typically precipitated by eating and lessens or resolves with fasting, which helps distinguish it from secretory (e.g., enterotoxigenic) diarrhea that persists during fasting (Harrison 22e p.2540-2541).

Celiac disease (celiac sprue / gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is a small-intestinal enteropathy from an immune response to gluten (wheat, rye, barley, some oats), characterized by autoantibodies to tissue transglutaminase; it primarily affects the proximal small bowel, so duodenal-limited disease may present as isolated iron-deficiency anemia while diffuse jejunal disease causes severe diarrhea, weight loss, and multinutrient malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2545).

Tissue transglutaminase IgA (TTG-IgA) is the celiac screening test of choice; serum IgA should be measured concurrently because IgA deficiency causes false-negative TTG-IgA, in which case IgG-based testing (TTG-IgG or anti-deamidated gliadin peptide DGP-IgG) is used (Harrison 22e p.2545).

In adults with positive celiac serology, diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy with small-intestinal biopsy showing villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; the Marsh classification grades severity (Harrison 22e p.2545).

PITFALL: celiac serologic and histologic testing must be performed while the patient is consuming gluten, since self-discontinuation of gluten before testing produces false-negative results; HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing is then useful because a negative result rules out celiac disease (negative predictive value >99%) (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545).

HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are necessary but not sufficient for celiac disease and are present in 25-35% of the general population, so their detection is NOT useful for diagnosis; their value lies in the very high negative predictive value when absent (Harrison 22e p.2544).

Dermatitis herpetiformis, a vesicular rash mediated by IgA skin deposits, is highly associated with celiac disease; celiac disease also carries increased risk of other autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease) and is more frequent in Down and Turner syndromes (Harrison 22e p.2545).

The mainstay of celiac treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with rigorous dietitian instruction; the most common cause of persistent symptoms or residual disease activity is dietary nonadherence or inadvertent gluten exposure (Harrison 22e p.2545-2546).

Tropical sprue presents with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies of BOTH folate and vitamin B12; malabsorption of two unrelated substances is required for diagnosis, and it is associated with residence in or travel to specific tropical regions (southern India, Pakistan, Philippines, Puerto Rico, Haiti, Cuba) (Harrison 22e p.2546-2547).

In India, tropical sprue is regarded by some as a postinfectious complication occurring in 8-20% of people after an attack of infectious gastroenteritis, with southern Indian patients often reporting acute enteritis preceding steatorrhea; tropical sprue is rarely seen in Africa, Jamaica, or Southeast Asia, and its overall incidence has declined (Harrison 22e p.2546-2547).

Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei, a PAS-positive non-acid-fast rod) most often affects middle-aged men; arthralgias/arthritis precede GI symptoms by an average of ~6 years (joint disease in >80%), and CNS and cardiac involvement occur later; diagnosis uses biopsy with PCR and PAS-positive macrophages (Harrison 22e p.2546).

Small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth arises from stasis (scleroderma, pseudo-obstruction, blind loops, strictures, diverticulosis) and from hypochlorhydria (chronic PPI use); it causes B12 deficiency (macrocytic anemia, peripheral neuropathy) from bacterial B12 metabolism, yet serum folate may be ELEVATED due to bacterial folate synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2543).

In ileal disease/resection, <100 cm involvement causes bile-acid spillage into the colon and secretory (cholerheic) diarrhea responsive to bile-acid sequestrants, whereas >100 cm exceeds hepatic synthetic capacity to replace lost bile acids, making fat malabsorption (steatorrhea) the dominant mechanism (Harrison 22e p.2542-2543).

Chronic pancreatitis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency cause voluminous steatorrhea with deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (most commonly D and K), and stool elastase is helpful for diagnosing pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2542, 2549).

In short-bowel/lipid malabsorption with an intact colon in continuity, luminal fatty acids saponify calcium, freeing oxalate for colonic absorption and increasing the risk of calcium-oxalate renal stones (hyperoxaluria) (Harrison 22e p.2548).
harrison.pathophysiology: Malabsorption results from disruption of one or more of the three phases of nutrient assimilation. (1) Luminal/digestive phase: intraluminal hydrolysis by gastric and pancreatic enzymes and solubilization of fat in bile-salt mixed micelles; impaired by postgastrectomy rapid transit, pancreatic insufficiency, hepatobiliary disease, ileal disease interrupting the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids, and small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth (which deconjugates bile acids causing luminal bile-acid deficiency). (2) Mucosal/absorptive phase: brush-border enzymatic digestion (disaccharidases, peptidases, enterokinase) and enterocyte uptake; impaired by isolated brush-border defects (lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption, sucrase-isomaltase deficiency) or by diffuse enteropathies (celiac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple's disease, Crohn's, infections). In celiac disease, tissue transglutaminase deamidates gluten-derived peptides, promoting their presentation by antigen-presenting cells in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 individuals, producing proximal villus atrophy with crypt hyperplasia; steatorrhea arises from mucosal malabsorption plus a secretory component from crypt hyperplasia/hypersecretion, and secondary lactase deficiency may develop. (3) Postmucosal/delivery phase: re-esterification of long-chain fatty acids into chylomicrons exiting via lymphatics; impaired by abetalipoproteinemia (failed chylomicron formation) and by lymphatic obstruction/dysfunction (lymphangiectasia, lymphoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis) or circulatory causes (Fontan physiology, constrictive pericarditis, CHF), which also cause protein-losing enteropathy. Specific nutrient deficiencies localize disease: duodenal/proximal disease causes iron and folate deficiency; ileal disease/resection causes B12 deficiency and bile-acid malabsorption; steatorrhea causes fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2540-2549).
additionalDifferentials: Chronic pancreatitis / exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Lactose intolerance from lactase deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2544)
Bile-acid (cholerheic) diarrhea from ileal disease/resection or primary bile-acid diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2543)
Crohn's disease with ileal involvement (Harrison 22e p.2542-2543)
Protein-losing enteropathy and intestinal lymphangiectasia (Harrison 22e p.2548-2549)
Environmental enteric dysfunction (formerly tropical enteropathy) (Harrison 22e p.2547)
infectionMimics: Tropical-environment enteric infections to exclude before diagnosing tropical sprue: Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium parvum, Cystoisospora (Isospora) belli, Strongyloides stercoralis, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Yersinia enterocolitica, Clostridioides difficile (Harrison 22e p.2547)
nonInfectiousMimics: Irritable bowel syndrome (celiac disease can mimic IBS; SIBO and bile-acid malabsorption occur in IBS-D) (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2546)
Intestinal lymphoma, including enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.2546)
Long-standing diabetes mellitus with enteric autonomic neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Scleroderma and other connective-tissue/motility disorders (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Menetrier's disease (hypertrophic gastropathy) as a cause of protein-losing enteropathy (Harrison 22e p.2549)
additionalInvestigations: 72-h quantitative fecal fat collection on a 100-g fat diet (gold standard for steatorrhea); qualitative spot Sudan III stain for fecal fat (Harrison 22e p.2549)
24-h stool weight/volume to confirm clinically significant diarrhea; stool osmotic gap (from spot fecal Na and K) to identify osmotic diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2549)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA (TTG-IgA) with concurrent serum total IgA; TTG-IgG or anti-deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP-IgG) if IgA-deficient (Harrison 22e p.2545)
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing chiefly to rule OUT celiac disease (high negative predictive value), especially if gluten was discontinued before testing (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545)
Endoscopy with small-intestinal (duodenal) biopsy; Marsh grading; in celiac, follow-up serology and a follow-up biopsy to document mucosal healing (Harrison 22e p.2545)
Stool elastase for pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2549)
SIBO testing: duodenal aspirate for bacterial titers (gold standard, limited availability) or lactulose/glucose breath hydrogen testing (interpret carefully for false positives) (Harrison 22e p.2543)
Lactose intolerance: lactose-exclusion diet trial, lactose-tolerance test (serum glucose rise <20 mg/L is positive), or breath hydrogen test (>20 ppm rise) (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545)
Protein-losing enteropathy: stool alpha-1 antitrypsin (spot or 24-h) or alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance; lymphopenia with hypoproteinemia supports GI protein loss (Harrison 22e p.2548-2549)
Whipple's disease: tissue PCR for T. whipplei, PAS staining, immunohistochemistry on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2546)

Labs reflecting site-specific deficiency: iron studies, B12 and folate, fat-soluble vitamins, PT/INR as a functional marker of vitamin K, serum carotene; cross-sectional imaging (MR enterography/CT), video capsule and double-balloon enteroscopy for occult mucosal/lymphatic disease (Harrison 22e p.2549)
redFlags: Persistent diarrhea, weight loss, and villus atrophy after >=1 year of a strict gluten-free diet with negative serology, indicating refractory celiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2546)

Type 2 refractory celiac disease (clonal CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gamma-chain rearrangement), which progresses to enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in 33-50% within 5 years (Harrison 22e p.2546)
New or worsening malabsorption with abdominal mass/imaging lymphadenopathy suggesting small-bowel adenocarcinoma or intestinal lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.2546)
Hypoproteinemia with peripheral edema, diarrhea, and lymphopenia (protein-losing enteropathy) requiring exclusion of cardiac and lymphatic causes (Harrison 22e p.2548)
Severe vitamin K deficiency causing coagulopathy (elevated PT/INR) and significant B12-related peripheral neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.2549)
Whipple's disease relapse, frequently heralding first CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.2546)
harrison.prognosis: Most patients with celiac disease respond fully to a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with mucosal healing and symptom resolution; about 10% of those with persistent active disease develop refractory celiac disease, and type 2 refractory disease carries a poor prognosis with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in 33-50% of cases at 5 years (requiring intensive chemotherapy and sometimes stem cell transplantation). Tropical sprue is most often curative with broad-spectrum antibiotics plus folic acid, especially if the patient leaves the tropical area and does not return. Whipple's disease requires prolonged antibiotics, but relapses are common. In short-bowel syndrome the intestine adapts over up to 2 years (with reports of continued improvement at 3-5 years); prognosis and parenteral-nutrition dependence relate to the extent of resection, presence of colon in continuity, and retention of the ileocecal valve, with intestinal failure defined by persistent parenteral-nutrition dependence (Harrison 22e p.2542-2548).
pitfalls: Testing for celiac disease (serology and biopsy) only after the patient has already self-removed gluten gives false-negative results; testing must be done ON a gluten-containing diet, or use HLA-DQ2/DQ8 to exclude disease (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545).

Interpreting HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positivity as diagnostic of celiac disease is wrong, as 25-35% of the general population carry these alleles without disease; only a negative result is clinically useful (rules out) (Harrison 22e p.2544).
Missing IgA deficiency when only TTG-IgA is ordered will produce false-negative celiac screening; order total serum IgA and use IgG-based tests if deficient (Harrison 22e p.2545).

Diagnosing tropical sprue before excluding enteric infection: it should NOT be entertained until cysts and trophozoites are excluded in three stool samples, and a gluten-free diet does NOT improve tropical sprue (unlike celiac disease) (Harrison 22e p.2547).

Breath hydrogen testing for lactose intolerance or SIBO can be inaccurate with abnormal gastric emptying or transit, and SIBO can itself produce false-positive/abnormal breath tests and mimic lactose intolerance (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2545).
In SIBO, expecting low folate is a trap; serum folate may be ELEVATED from bacterial synthesis while B12 is low (Harrison 22e p.2543).

In protein-losing enteropathy, isolated low albumin with normal globulins suggests renal/hepatic disease rather than GI loss; alpha-1 antitrypsin cannot assess gastric protein loss because it is degraded in acid (Harrison 22e p.2548-2549).
Treating the hypoproteinemia of protein-losing enteropathy directly rather than the underlying disease is misdirected; therapy should target the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.2549).
harrison.severityClassification: There is no single unified severity scale for malabsorption; severity is assessed by the degree of nutrient deficiency and steatorrhea and by disease-specific schemes. Celiac mucosal injury is graded by the Marsh classification of biopsy lesions (intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and degrees of villus atrophy). Celiac complications are stratified into refractory celiac disease type 1 (normal intraepithelial lymphocyte population, better prognosis) versus type 2 (clonal CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gamma rearrangement, worse prognosis with high lymphoma risk). Bile-acid versus fatty-acid diarrhea are distinguished by extent of ileal disease (<100 cm vs >100 cm), degree of steatorrhea, and response to cholestyramine versus a low-fat diet. Short-bowel syndrome is defined as <200 cm of remaining small bowel, and intestinal failure as persistent parenteral-nutrition dependence (generally <100 cm of small bowel with no colon in continuity) (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2545-2548).
management: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment for coeliac disease, supported by a specialist dietitian
Correct nutritional deficiencies with iron, folate, vitamin B12, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and calcium replacement
Give pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy with meals for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
Treat small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth with a course of appropriate antibiotics such as rifaximin, and use bile-acid sequestrants for bile-acid malabsorption
Restrict lactose or the relevant sugar in brush-border disaccharidase deficiencies
Monitor response with follow-up coeliac serology and, where indicated, repeat duodenal biopsy to document mucosal healing
For refractory coeliac disease use corticosteroids or immunosuppression and evaluate for enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma
Offer serological screening to first-degree relatives of patients with coeliac disease
